sources.title: How to Use an Aquarium Air Pump (and Make Them Quieter)
How to Care for Your Aquarium Fish During a Power Outage
How to Keep Your Aquarium Fish Alive During A Power Outage
Water Quality and its Impact on Diseases of Fish
Máy sủi oxy bị vào nước: Nguyên nhân và cách xử lý an toàn hiệu quả
Máy sủi oxy có tốn điện không? Có nên bật liên tục cho hồ cá?

facts.fact: An aquarium air pump sits outside the tank and pushes air through airline tubing to devices inside, such as air stones, sponge filters and decorations.
Rising bubbles move the water and stir the surface. Surface agitation is the key to gas exchange: CO2 leaves the water and oxygen dissolves in.
Not every tank needs an air pump. Hang-on-back and canister filters have their own motors, but sponge and undergravel filters run on air and need a pump.
Other uses for an air pump include corner box filters, moving bed filters, breeder boxes and egg tumblers.
Oxygen enters water from the plants and algae that make it during photosynthesis, and from the air by diffusion at the surface.
Wind, waves and mechanical aerators enlarge the water's surface area, which speeds up oxygen diffusion.
Tropical fish generally need 6 to 10 ppm dissolved oxygen, and most fish become stressed below 6 ppm.
Oxygen below 2 mg/L stresses fish and raises the risk of illness or death. Warm-water fish need about 5 mg/L for best health.
Aquarium Co-Op generally recommends running the air pump all the time for circulation and oxygen.
When water is short of oxygen (hypoxia), fish gather at the surface and gasp, which aquarists call 'piping'. Without correction, it can be fatal.
Warmer water holds less oxygen: about 7.4 mg/L at 90°F compared with about 11.9 mg/L at 45°F.
In warm water, fish are more active and use oxygen faster.
Oxygen falls after sunset as photosynthesis slows, and fish kills in ponds often happen around 4 to 6 a.m., just before dawn.
Plants make oxygen by day but use it at night. Lewbart notes this rarely causes oxygen depletion in home aquariums.
Dissolved oxygen also falls as salinity rises and as atmospheric pressure drops.

Water flowing back into an air pump is usually caused by one of these: the pump sits below the water level, there is no check valve or it is broken, the tubing is cracked or loose, or the pump is in a damp place near the tank.
A check valve on the airline keeps water from siphoning back out of the tank if the power fails. It is needed only when the pump sits lower than the top of the tank.
Fit the check valve so its flapper faces the pump.
Make a drip loop in the pump's power cord so water cannot run along it into the outlet.
Lewbart's aeration guideline is 6 to 8 liters of air per hour for every 3.8 liters (1 gallon) of water.
For power cuts, keep a USB air pump that can run from a power bank or laptop, or a pump with a built-in battery.
A battery air pump with an air stone can stand in for the mains pump that runs your air-driven filters or air stones during an outage.
If water gets into an air pump, unplug it at once to avoid a short circuit or electric shock.

To dry a wet air pump: unplug it, tip the water out (open the case if you can), and let it dry in a ventilated place for 1–2 days. A hair dryer on the cool setting also works. Then test it for a few minutes. Replace it if it does not run or smells burnt.
In a power cut, leave the tank alone for the first 1–2 hours: do not feed, turn off auto feeders, and do not change water.
If the power is out for more than 8 hours, run a battery air pump for about an hour every 8 hours. Run it every 4 hours if the tank is overstocked or fish are gasping.
A pump in battery Power Save mode (air 15 s on, 15 s off) runs longer than one running nonstop, and lower airflow stretches battery life further.
During an outage, unplug hang-on-back and canister filters so that rotting debris is not flushed into the tank when power returns. Some keepers move the filter media into the tank.
In hot weather during an outage, move the tank somewhere cool and shaded. A battery fan blowing across the water cools it by evaporation.
After power returns, test for ammonia and nitrite and change water if either is above 0 ppm. Clean the filter media before plugging filters back in.
After power returns, wait 24 hours before feeding.
Do not feed during an outage. Afterwards, wait about 24 hours or until water quality is normal, then feed smaller portions. Most fish can go about a week without food.
Floating frozen water bottles to cool a tank is a mistake: the ice melts fast and can cause sudden temperature swings.
Overaerating very warm water to make up for low oxygen can supersaturate it and cause gas bubble disease. The fix is to control temperature and adjust aeration.
Diaphragm air pumps vibrate and get louder with age. To quiet one, cushion it, set it on a solid surface, hang it by its cord, or clean clogged air stones.
Dissolved oxygen test kits are sold at most good pet stores.
Cooler water holds more oxygen, and surface agitation helps gas exchange.

Vietnamese names: máy sủi oxy (air pump), van một chiều (check valve), ống dẫn khí or dây oxy (airline tubing), đá sủi (air stone), van chia khí (air valve), máy sủi oxy tích điện (rechargeable pump).
Brands sold in Vietnam include Resun, Atman, Sunsun and Hailea (for example the Hailea ACO series).
A Vietnamese shop says most air pumps on sale draw 2–10W, typically 3–5W. This is a seller's figure.
A Vietnamese shop advises plugging the pump into an outlet with a residual-current (earth-leakage) breaker (ổ cắm có cầu dao chống rò điện).
